Lofgren (D-CA) introduced a federal comprehensive privacy bill, Oklahoma’s comprehensive privacy bill has been sent to the governor for signature, the Kentucky House passed a privacy amendment concerning smart TVs, and the Vermont House passed a neural data bill. 💬 New Resource on U.S. Regulatory Approach to Voluntary AI Governance Standards: FPF U.S. Policy Intern Rafal Fryc has published a new blog post on the U.S. regulatory approach to voluntary AI governance standards (e.g., NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework or ISO 42001). The blog post highlights the growth of AI laws utilizing voluntary standards, pending legislation, and how courts are using frameworks like NIST's AI RMF to define the standard of care in negligence and strict liability cases. 

 

Stuff from the States 

 

California - ‘Vehicle Telematics for Insurance’ Bill Introduced (AB 1833): The California Assembly amended AB 1833 this week to convert the bill into an amendment to the Insurance Code. As originally introduced, this bill would have made technical changes to the definition of “connected vehicle location access” under the Vehicle Code. As amended, this bill would allow consumers to opt-in to the use of telematics to establish a driving record for insurance purposes. Insurers would be prohibited from requiring participation in such a program as a condition of obtaining or renewing coverage, penalizing a consumer who declines to participate, or increasing a premium in increments of less than six months from the date the policy goes into effect. 

 

Connecticut - General Law Committee Approved Substitute for CTDPA Amendment (SB 4): The General Law Committee voted on March 16 to approve a joint favorable substitute to SB 4, a CTDPA amendment. The substitute includes numerous technical changes to the Delete Act-style data broker provisions, a small adjustment to the limit on facial recognition technology for security purposes (relevant to employee-only areas), removing some of the specific requirements for the proposed algorithmic pricing disclosure, and a new prohibition on using an electronic pricing label with personalized algorithmic pricing to increase the price for a specific consumer good to be sold as part of an in-person transaction. 

 

Illinois - Hearings on Numerous Privacy Bills this Week: A number of privacy bills had or will have hearings this week—including comprehensive privacy bills HB HB 3041 and HB 5221, neural data and BIPA amendment bill HB 2984, and genetic testing and biomarker bill HB 4556. This is a notable flurry of activity, particularly as several of these bills had been inactive since being introduced last year.

 

Kentucky - KCDPA Amendment on Smart TVs Passed House (HB 692): The House passed HB 692 on March 13 by a vote of 92-0. This bill would amend the KCDPA to add “automatic content recognition data” (data captured by a smart television or smart monitor) as a category of sensitive data.

 

Louisiana - ASAA Amendment Introduced (HB 977): This bill was introduced by Rep. Beaullieu (R) on March 17 and would amend the Louisiana ASAA to address some of the constitutional concerns that have been raised against last year’s iteration of this framework. Changes to the law would include adding parental consent obligations for accessing pre-installed apps and removing  application exemptions (both of which were factors in the preliminary injunction analysis against Texas’ law).

 

Minnesota 

  • AADC-Style Bill Introduced (SF 4574): Sen. Maye Quade (D) introduced this AADC bill on March 18. Largely aligning with the Maryland model, this bill includes a “best interests of children” fiduciary duty and would require companies to conduct DPIAs, restrict certain data management practices such as precise geolocation data processing, configure all default privacy settings to a high level of privacy for children, and provide any privacy information or terms of service in clear, age-appropriate language.
  • Data Broker Bill Introduced (HF 4456): Rep. Elkins (D) has introduced a data broker bill. This bill would require data brokers to register with the state annually and the attorney general to make registrants’ information available on a public website. 

 

Oklahoma - Comprehensive Privacy Bill Sent to Governor (SB 546): Oklahoma is close to becoming the 20th U.S. state to enact a comprehensive consumer privacy bill, as SB 546 passed its fourth reading and was sent to the governor on March 17. Governor Stitt has 5 days to sign or veto (excluding Sundays), so that deadline should be this upcoming Monday. You can find a two-page overview of the bill—which closely adheres to the Virginia model—on the FPF Portal. 

 

Vermont

  • Data Broker Bill Amended & Re-referred (H.211): The House Committee on Commerce and Economic Development reported a substitute to H.211 on March 17. This bill now moves to the Ways & Means Committee. The introduced version of this bill would have updated Vermont's data broker registry law and created a California-style “accessible deletion mechanism.” While this bill still includes a requirement for data brokers to comply with consumer deletion requests, this new draft would not create an accessible deletion mechanism; rather, it would direct the Secretary of State to study the feasibility of doing so. Amongst the other changes in the new draft are altered definitions (e.g., aligning the definition of “brokered personal information” more closely with definitions of “personal data” under comprehensive privacy laws and aligning “data broker” with the definition in the California Delete Act). The effective date has been changed to January 1, 2027.
  • Neural Data Bill Passed House (H.814): The House passed H.814 on March 18. This bill would give consumers rights over the collection or recording of an individual's neural data gathered from a brain-computer interface. 

Federal Happenings

 

Rep. Lofgren (D-CA) Introduced Federal Privacy Bill: Recent weeks have seen an uptick in federal legislative activity on privacy and artificial intelligence. Continuing that trend, Rep. Lofgren (D-CA) released a comprehensive privacy bill on March 19. This is not the Republican-led bill that we have been anticipating from the House Energy & Commerce Committee. The bill includes many protections and requirements that go beyond what is typical of the state landscape, including: broad consumer rights (e.g., human review of impactful automated decisions, opt-in consent for using data for machine learning or AI algorithms, and decisions with respect to how long personal information is retained); substantive data minimization obligations that require a “reasonable, articulated basis” for processing personal information that balances the business’s needs against the potential privacy harms to a consumer and a consumer’s reasonable expectations; and the establishment of a new Digital Privacy Agency to issue regulations and enforce the bill. 

 

Rep. Blackburn (R-TN) Released Federal AI Bill Discussion Draft: Rep. Blackburn (R-TN) released a discussion draft of a federal AI bill on March 18. As covered in our Thursday newsletter on AI Legislation, this discussion draft aims to establish a national AI framework that would codify elements of President Trump’s executive order on artificial intelligence and incorporate several previously introduced bills from other senators. Notably, the draft also included the Senate version of the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA), which is also sponsored by Rep. Blackburn and aims to provide online safety protections to minors by: establishing a duty for covered platforms to exercise reasonable care to mitigate risks of harm to minors; providing certain safeguards to minors such as limits on other communication from other users; restricting personalized recommendation systems; and requiring public reporting disclosures.
